howItWorks.intro: Behind the single number is simple addition, not a hidden algorithm. Close relationships are multiplied by 5 and capped at 25 points; weekly meaningful interactions are multiplied by 3 and capped at 25 points, which means the interaction score maxes out once you report roughly 8 to 9 contacts in a week; your self-rated belonging (1-10) is multiplied by 2.5 for up to 25 points; and your loneliness-frequency selection maps directly to a fixed point value — 25 for "Rarely," 15 for "Sometimes," 5 for "Often," 0 for "Always." The four subtotals are summed for a score out of 100.

rules.name: Social Score
rules.formula: Score = Relationships + Interactions + Belonging + Loneliness factors

howItWorks.outro: That 0-100 total sorts into four bands: 80 and above reads as strong social health, 60-79 as adequate with room for deeper connections, 40-59 as at-risk and worth prioritizing social activity, and below 40 as concerning enough to consider reaching out for support. Because two of the four inputs are self-ratings (belonging and loneliness frequency), the same real-life week could produce different scores for two people who'd describe their social life identically — treat the band as a prompt for reflection, not a precise ranking against anyone else's number.

faq.question: Why are close relationships and weekly interactions capped instead of scored without a ceiling?
faq.answer: Both inputs stop adding points past a threshold — 5 relationships and roughly 8-9 weekly interactions — because the scoring is built around research suggesting a small, stable circle of contact matters more than raw volume. Robin Dunbar's work on relationship layers puts the closest support group at around five people; beyond that, added contacts don't reliably keep adding the same wellbeing benefit.

faq.question: Is this the same as a clinical loneliness or depression screening?
faq.answer: No. It's a self-reflection tool built from four self-reported inputs, not a validated instrument like the UCLA Loneliness Scale or a clinical depression screener. It can flag a pattern worth paying attention to, but it can't diagnose anything, and it shouldn't replace a conversation with a doctor or therapist if isolation is affecting your daily life.

faq.question: What does a score around 60 actually mean?
faq.answer: 60 sits at the bottom of the "adequate" band (60-79), which generally reflects some real connection alongside room to deepen it — for example, 3 close relationships, 5 weekly interactions, a belonging rating of 6, and "Sometimes" feeling lonely produces exactly 60. It's not a failing score; it's closer to a nudge that one or two subscores have headroom.

faq.question: My belonging score feels subjective — how should I rate it?
faq.answer: Rate it against how connected you feel to a specific group, workplace, or community over the past few weeks, not against an abstract ideal or against how you think you should feel. If you genuinely can't decide between two numbers, pick the lower one and rerun the calculator later to see whether it moves.

faq.question: How often should I recheck my score?
faq.answer: Every few weeks, or after a change in circumstances like a move or a new job, is enough to see a real trend. Running it multiple times a day mostly captures mood swings rather than a genuine shift in your social connection, and persistent low scores are better addressed by talking to someone than by repeated recalculation.

howWeCalculate.intro: Nothing here is sent to a server or averaged against other users — the four numbers you enter are combined in your browser using the fixed weights described above, and the result disappears the moment you close the tab.
steps: Count close relationships honestly, using people you could call with bad news at 3 a.m., not your full contact list or social media followers
Estimate meaningful interactions for a typical week — conversations with actual back-and-forth, not texts you only reacted to with an emoji

Rate your sense of belonging from 1 to 10 based on how connected you feel to a group, community, or set of people right now, then pick the loneliness-frequency option that best matches the last few weeks
Click Calculate to see the composite score and its band, then compare it against how you'd have described your own social life before running the numbers
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: This is a self-reported composite, not a validated psychological instrument — treat a low score as a nudge to reach out or reflect, and treat a persistently low score as a reason to talk with a professional rather than a verdict to accept at face value.

whenToUse.intro: The four inputs respond quickly to real changes in circumstance, which makes this most useful at specific moments rather than as a running daily habit.
scenarios: After a move, job change, breakup, or retirement, when your usual sources of contact have shifted and you want a baseline to track
When you notice yourself canceling plans repeatedly and want a number to check that impression against
During a stretch of high work or caregiving load, to see whether meaningful interactions have quietly dropped to zero
Before deciding whether to invest more time in existing relationships or to actively seek new ones, since the relationship and interaction subscores point in different directions
As an occasional pulse-check every few weeks — rerunning it daily will mostly just measure noise in a single day's mood

sections.title: What the Four Inputs Actually Measure
sections.body: This calculator turns four separate inputs into a single 0-100 composite: close relationships, meaningful interactions in a typical week, a self-rated sense of belonging (1-10), and how often loneliness shows up. Each input converts to points on its own scale, then the four scores are added together — relationships and weekly interactions are each capped at 25 points, belonging tops out at 25 points when rated a perfect 10, and loneliness frequency contributes a fixed amount depending on which of four options you pick, from 25 points for "Rarely" down to 0 for "Always." The caps are deliberate, not accidental: past a certain point, adding more contacts or more check-ins doesn't keep adding the same marginal benefit, so the scoring reflects diminishing returns rather than treating a 20th acquaintance the same as a 1st close friend.

sections.title: The Research Behind the Relationship Cap
sections.body: The five-relationship ceiling on the close-relationships input isn't arbitrary — it echoes anthropologist Robin Dunbar's layered model of relationship capacity, which puts the innermost "support clique" (people you'd call at 3 a.m.) at roughly five, a close-friend layer at around fifteen, and a wider circle of maintained relationships topping out near 150. Consider two people running the numbers. Person A logs 3 close relationships, 5 meaningful interactions that week, rates belonging a 6 out of 10, and picks "Sometimes" for loneliness. That works out to relationship points of 3 × 5 = 15, interaction points of 5 × 3 = 15, belonging points of 6 × 2.5 = 15, and loneliness points of 15 for "Sometimes" — a total of 60, landing in the "Adequate — room for deeper connections" band. Person B logs 1 close relationship, 1 weekly interaction, a belonging score of 3, and picks "Often" for loneliness: 1 × 5 = 5, 1 × 3 = 3, 3 × 2.5 = 7.5, plus 5 for "Often," totaling roughly 21 and landing in the "Concerning" band. The gap between those two scores isn't about one person having more free time than the other — it's about the density and reliability of contact each one reports.

sections.title: A Self-Check, Not a Diagnosis
sections.body: This score is a structured way to reflect on your own social patterns, modeled loosely on the domains the 2023 U.S. Surgeon General's advisory on loneliness and isolation flagged as relevant to health — not a validated clinical instrument like the UCLA Loneliness Scale, and it does not diagnose loneliness, social anxiety, or depression. Public health research has repeatedly linked chronic social isolation to elevated risks for cardiovascular disease, stroke, and early mortality on a scale researchers have compared to smoking roughly a pack a day, which is part of why a numeric check-in like this one is worth taking seriously. If your score keeps landing in the lower bands over several weeks, or if loneliness is affecting your sleep, work, or motivation, treat that as a reason to talk to a doctor, therapist, or someone you trust — not as something a self-scored calculator can resolve on its own.

howToSteps.title: Count Your Close Relationships
howToSteps.description: Enter the number of people you'd call your closest support — the calculator caps this input's contribution at 5, so anything above that won't add further points.

howToSteps.title: Estimate Weekly Meaningful Interactions
howToSteps.description: Enter roughly how many real conversations or check-ins you have in a typical week; this input caps out around 8-9 interactions.

howToSteps.title: Rate Belonging and Loneliness Frequency
howToSteps.description: Score your sense of belonging from 1 to 10, then choose the loneliness-frequency option — Rarely, Sometimes, Often, or Always — that best fits recent weeks.

howToSteps.title: Calculate and Read the Band
howToSteps.description: Click Calculate to get your 0-100 score and its band, from "Strong social health" down to "Concerning" — then use the breakdown above to see which subscore is pulling the total down.

tips: Count close relationships, not total contacts — the cap sits at 5 because the score is built around Dunbar's inner "support clique," not your full address book.
Weekly interactions cap out at 25 points once you hit roughly 8 to 9 in a week, so there's no benefit to inflating the number past that — accuracy below the cap matters more.
Rate belonging based on the last few weeks, not a single good or bad day — a single argument or a single great dinner will skew a one-day snapshot.
Pick the loneliness-frequency option that matches your honest pattern rather than the one that sounds better; the score is only useful if the inputs are accurate.
If your result lands in the "concerning" or "at-risk" band more than once, treat that as a cue to talk to someone rather than a reason to keep re-running the calculator.
